domain_label: Turlock & Central Valley Home & Contractor Trades Supply Chain and Operating Model
purpose: A session-bounded method for an independent Turlock home-and-trades operator to design, set up, and harden the operating system of a truck-and-tools service business across its inputs (devices, fixtures, condensers, water heaters, flooring goods, irrigation, chemicals), its shared supply-house universe (Graybar/Rexel/CED electrical, Ferguson/Hajoca/PACE plumbing, Watsco/Johnstone HVAC, Shaw/Mohawk flooring, SiteOne/Ewing landscape, WAXIE/Imperial Dade janitorial), its equipment and vehicle capex, its license-tied labor model, and its CSLB/permit regulatory gates, by mapping the binding cost center per sub-category, choosing the right channel and labor archetype, exploiting the no-rent mobile profile, clearing the licensing and bonding gates, and building resilience against skilled-labor scarcity, Modesto leakage, and the SB 216/SB 1455 workers-comp cost-shock.
assumptions: no per-operator job-costing or purchasing dataset is supplied; channel mixes, labor-share weights, and capex bands are reasoned heuristic priors keyed to the home_trades deep-dive, not invoices
the operator runs one of the 22 independent Turlock firms profiled in the deep-dive across six sub-categories (electrical, flooring, HVAC, janitorial/cleaning, landscaping, plumbing)
the geography is Turlock / Stanislaus County in the Modesto MSA, ~15 miles from Modesto's larger trade firms and supply houses, in an aging 1950s-1990s housing stock, in 2026

supplier-to-named-business links are representative inference, not confirmed accounts, unless the deep-dive cites the relationship; the shared supply houses serve every local firm so there is no supply-side moat in the crowded segments

per-business dollar revenue is never asserted; any dollar figure is a labeled benchmark estimate (per-truck/per-tech/per-employee benchmark x an observable size signal x sub-category band) tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path
the licensed operator holds or is obtaining the required CSLB classification tied to a Responsible Managing Officer, the $25,000 contractor bond, and workers' compensation where employees are present
exclusions: per-business revenue, profit, or market-share actuals stated as fact (only labeled benchmark estimates and cited public CSLB/bond/fee figures are used)
front-of-customer sales, bidding strategy, and estimating workflow beyond naming the $1,000 CSLB threshold and the cost-center inputs a bid must cover
site selection and the flooring-showroom lease/buildout financing decision beyond the equipment-and-vehicle capex node
marketing, lead generation, demand forecasting, and saturation/white-space strategy (covered by the market-saturation KB)
detailed wage bands, hiring funnels, and apprenticeship pipelines beyond the license-tied labor-model and skilled-labor-scarcity nodes
household financing/HELOC mechanics and homeowner credit beyond naming demand's out-of-pocket, rate-sensitive character

competency_questions.question: For this specific Turlock trade sub-category, what is the binding cost center, and which inputs or constraints must the operating plan protect first?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUBCATEGORY_COST_PROFILE names the sub-category's binding cost center from the deep-dive (e.g., skilled journeyman labor for electrical/plumbing/HVAC, a single condenser/water-heater/panel equipment hit per job, special-order flooring goods for flooring, crew-hours for janitorial, labor-at-40-50%-of-revenue for landscape maintenance) and ranks the remaining inputs by cost share and risk

competency_questions.question: What is the realistic, shared supply-house universe verified to serve Turlock/Modesto/Central Valley, and how is it segmented by trade?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUPPLY_HOUSE_UNIVERSE enumerates the electrical, plumbing, HVAC, flooring, landscape, and janitorial branch-wholesaler nodes named in the deep-dive, tags each verified-to-serve vs representative inference, and states that the houses are shared across local firms so there is no supply-side moat

competency_questions.question: Which CSLB classification, bond, and workers-comp gates must clear before the operator can legally bid covered work, and which sub-categories are barely gated?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LICENSING_GATE cites the $1,000 covered-work rule, the relevant C-10/C-20/C-36/C-27/C-15 classes tied to an RMO, the $25k bond and $100k LLC worker bond, the WC requirement (and C-20's no-exemption rule), and flags janitorial as generally non-CSLB-gated

competency_questions.question: What is the two-engine operating model, and how does it sort a firm into a licensed-moat path or an easy-entry recurring-service path?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OPERATING_MODEL_ENGINE contrasts Engine A (licensed, event-driven mechanical trades with license/bond/WC/skilled-labor moats) against Engine B (easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring janitorial/landscape) and routes the operator to the right defensibility logic

competency_questions.question: How does an operator exploit the no-rent mobile truck-and-tools capital profile rather than a storefront inventory model?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MOBILE_CAPITAL_PROFILE explains the vans-plus-specialized-tools, near-zero-held-inventory, just-in-time-from-the-supply-house profile the deep-dive documents, and names flooring's showroom as the lone storefront exception

competency_questions.question: How is just-in-time branch-wholesaler material flow set up on trade credit for the mechanical trades, and what are the stocked vs special-order lead times?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: JIT_TRADE_CREDIT describes drawing exact pipe/wire/fittings/condensers from a local supply-house branch on a trade-credit account with same-day-to-next-day stocked lead time and weeks-to-months special-order (switchgear, tankless, full HVAC systems)

competency_questions.question: How is the licensed mechanical-trade input chain (electrical devices/gear, plumbing fixtures/heaters, HVAC condensers/refrigerant) sourced and its per-job equipment hit managed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MECHANICAL_TRADE_INPUTS routes electrical (Graybar/CED, Square D/Eaton gear), plumbing (Hajoca/Ferguson/PACE, Rheem/Bradford White heaters), and HVAC (Watsco/Johnstone, condensers/refrigerant) inputs and addresses the large single-equipment-purchase exposure per job

competency_questions.question: How is the flooring showroom-plus-install model sourced, the sector's one storefront/special-order inventory exception?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FLOORING_SHOWROOM_MODEL names the manufacturer goods (Shaw/Mohawk/Mannington) sampled in a showroom (Arrow, Turlock Floor Covering), the ~1-3 week special-order cut-to-job lead time, and the install-crew dispatch with low warehoused stock

competency_questions.question: How is the easy-entry labor model (janitorial crews, landscape maintenance) set up where labor is the product and the moat is contract retention?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LABOR_IS_PRODUCT_MODEL explains the recurring-contract route-crew model (janitorial 50-60% labor, landscape maintenance 40-50% labor), the thin shared supply (WAXIE/SiteOne), and that defensibility is contract retention not capital

competency_questions.question: How is the 24/7 emergency-dispatch and seasonal-surge operating premium set up, and why is after-hours repair the highest-margin work?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: EMERGENCY_DISPATCH covers 24/7 plumbing/HVAC dispatch (PRO Plumbers, Turlock Plumbing Co) across Stanislaus County, the summer-100F HVAC cooling-failure surge, and that repair gross (35-55%) exceeds install gross

competency_questions.question: How are permits, inspections, and chemical-applicator/OSHA/DOT compliance set up as recurring operational gates, not one-time events?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PERMIT_INSPECTION specifies City of Turlock/Stanislaus County building permits for panels/water-heaters/repipes/HVAC-changeouts, backflow testing, EPA 608, DPR/county-Ag chemical-applicator licensing for landscape pesticide, and Cal/OSHA/DOT exposure

competency_questions.question: How is per-business revenue and margin modeled honestly without asserting any named firm's actuals, and how does the operator harden against skilled-labor scarcity, Modesto leakage, and the WC cost-shock on a review cadence?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COST_BENCHMARK_HONESTY derives revenue/margin as a labeled estimate (per-truck/per-tech benchmark x size signal x band) tagged estimate-not-actual; RESILIENCE_BACKUP names backups for skilled labor, key equipment, and supply; OPERATIONS_REVIEW_LOOP sets a review cadence and the triggers (labor loss, WC landing, price spike) that re-run the plan

glossary.definition: A California Contractors State License Board specialty license tied to a Responsible Managing Officer that legally authorizes covered work: C-10 electrical (AEI #885461, Frayer #1101008), C-20 HVAC (Horizon, Saunders), C-36 plumbing (Johnson, Mainline, PRO), C-27 landscaping, C-15 flooring, C-8 concrete (Capote); required for any project where labor plus materials reaches $1,000.

A local trade distributor branch (Graybar/CED for electrical, Ferguson/Hajoca/PACE for plumbing, Watsco/Johnstone for HVAC, SiteOne/Ewing for landscape, WAXIE for janitorial) from which a contractor draws exact materials on a trade-credit account, just-in-time for booked work; shared across all local firms so it confers no supply-side moat.

An open net-terms account a licensed contractor holds at a supply house, drawing pipe, wire, fittings, fixtures, or condensers for booked jobs and paying on terms rather than at the counter; the financing backbone that lets a no-inventory mobile firm operate with same-day-to-next-day stocked material.

The sector's defining no-rent mobile capital base: service vans and specialized tools (testers, benders, drain machines, recovery machines, mowers) with near-zero held finished-goods inventory, drawing material JIT from the supply house; the flooring showroom is the lone storefront/inventory exception.

The mandatory CSLB contractor surety bond every licensee must keep on file (an LLC carries an additional $100,000 worker bond); a cited fixed regulatory gate, paid as an annual premium, that filters casual entrants out of the licensed trades alongside skilled-labor scarcity.

The federal refrigerant-handling certification HVAC technicians must hold to service air-conditioning systems; coupled with A2L refrigerant-transition rules it gates HVAC equipment purchasing and technician capability for C-20 firms such as Horizon and Saunders.

The California push toward workers-compensation-for-all-licensees (SB 216), deferred from 1/1/2026 to 1/1/2028 by SB 1455; a near-term fixed-cost shock the deep-dive flags as raising the entry bar further for the smallest licensed operators when it lands.

The deep-dive's spine: Engine A is the licensed, event-driven mechanical trades (electrical, HVAC, plumbing) with real license/bond/WC/skilled-labor moats and non-discretionary demand; Engine B is the easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring services (janitorial, landscape maintenance) where defensibility is contract retention, not capital.

A revenue/margin figure built as a published per-truck/per-technician/per-employee productivity benchmark times an observable size signal (years in business, residential-vs-commercial mix, fleet/crew language, showroom presence) times the sub-category band, explicitly tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path; never a claim of a named firm's actual revenue.

The structural cap on the Turlock-headquartered firm count from Modesto (~218k residents, 15 miles north) hosting larger trade firms, supply houses, national/franchise players, and big-box installed services (Home Depot/Lowe's flooring, water heaters, HVAC) that absorb high-ticket and specialty jobs north.

nodes.definition: Pin down, for the operator's specific Turlock trade sub-category, which input or constraint is the binding cost center and how the remaining inputs rank by spend and risk: skilled journeyman/apprentice labor for electrical/plumbing/HVAC (a hard supply constraint, not just a cost line), a single large equipment purchase per job (a condenser for HVAC, a water heater for plumbing, a panel/switchgear for electrical), special-order manufacturer goods for flooring (Shaw/Mohawk product is cut-to-job), and crew-hours for the labor-is-the-product services (janitorial at 50-60% of revenue, landscape maintenance at 40-50%). This profile is the raw input that bounds every supplier, capex, and labor choice downstream.

included: input ranking by cost share and risk
the inputs or labor constraint the plan must protect first

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the sub-category, service mix, or binding cost center changes

pros.claim: Naming the one binding cost center focuses operating effort where margin is actually won or lost
pros.example: an electrical firm that recognizes skilled-electrician availability as its binding constraint prioritizes apprentice pipeline over chasing cheaper devices at the supply house

cons.claim: Over-fixating on the single biggest cost center can starve attention from a smaller input with higher stockout or per-job-spike risk
cons.example: an HVAC firm optimizing labor scheduling while a refrigerant or condenser special-order delay strands a changeout job mid-July

failure_modes: importing another sub-category's cost profile so the wrong constraint is protected
treating labor-dominant janitorial or landscape maintenance as a materials problem when crew-hours dominate
acceptance_tests: the profile names the sub-category's binding cost center exactly as the deep-dive marks it and ranks at least three more inputs or constraints by cost share and risk
revisit_triggers: the operator adds a sub-category line (e.g., a plumber cross-selling HVAC like DeHart)
a previously minor input becomes the binding cost or risk

nodes.definition: Enumerate the realistic branch-wholesaler universe verified to serve Turlock/Modesto/Central Valley and segment it by trade: electrical (Graybar, Rexel/Platt, CED, Ferguson Electrical, Border States), plumbing (Hajoca, Ferguson Plumbing, PACE Supply, Morrison Supply), HVAC (Ferguson HVAC, Watsco/Carrier Enterprise, Johnstone Supply, LennoxPros), flooring (Shaw, Mohawk, Mannington, Engineered Floors and regional distributors), landscape (SiteOne, Ewing, Horizon Distributors carrying Hunter/Rain Bird/Toro), and janitorial (WAXIE, Imperial Dade, CleanSource, Uline). Each node is tagged verified-to-serve-this-geography versus representative inference; the decisive insight is that these houses are shared across every local firm, so there is no supply-side moat in the crowded segments.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the verified supply-house set or its Turlock reach changes

pros.claim: A pre-mapped, geography-verified supply-house list stops the operator from cold-calling distributors that do not stock or deliver to the county
pros.example: knowing Ferguson and Hajoca both run plumbing branches serving Stanislaus County avoids chasing a Bay Area house with no local will-call

cons.claim: A fixed universe can ossify and miss a new branch opening or a distributor that recently extended delivery into the county
cons.example: overlooking a newly opened SiteOne yard because it postdates the deep-dive snapshot

failure_modes: treating an inferred supplier link as a confirmed account
assuming a supply-house relationship is a moat when every competitor draws from the same branch
acceptance_tests: the universe lists all six trade segments with at least one named, geography-verified branch-wholesaler each and tags every named link as verified or inference
revisit_triggers: a supply house opens, closes, merges, or changes its Turlock reach
a manufacturer changes its regional distribution

nodes.definition: Establish the CSLB licensing gate that legally precedes any covered bid: a license is required for any project where labor plus materials reaches $1,000 (the $1k rule), tied to a Responsible Managing Officer, in the relevant Class-C classification - C-10 electrical (AEI, Frayer), C-20 HVAC (Horizon, Saunders, and the HVAC side of DeHart and Turlock Plumbing H&A), C-36 plumbing (Johnson, Mainline, PRO, Turlock Plumbing Co, DeHart), C-27 landscaping (the seven landscapers, with Capote's concrete possibly invoking C-8), and C-15 flooring (Arrow, Turlock Floor Covering). Janitorial is generally not CSLB-gated, running instead on a city business license plus a liability/janitorial bond - the structural fact that makes it an easy-entry sub-category.

included: the C-class classification tied to an RMO per sub-category

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a CSLB classification scope or the covered-work threshold changes

pros.claim: Pricing the licensing gate up front prevents an operator from bidding covered work it cannot legally perform
pros.example: a would-be electrical firm confirming its C-10 RMO and license number before bidding a panel upgrade over the $1k threshold

cons.claim: Treating every sub-category as hard-gated over-states the entry barrier for a janitorial or commodity-mowing operator that needs only a city license
cons.example: a residential cleaning startup assuming it needs a CSLB classification it does not

failure_modes: bidding or performing covered work over $1,000 without the matching C-class
missing that a concrete cross-sell (Capote) may require a separate C-8 classification
acceptance_tests: the required C-class for the operator's sub-category is named with its RMO tie and the $1,000 threshold, and janitorial's non-gated status is stated where it applies
revisit_triggers: the operator adds a covered service line in a new classification
CSLB changes a classification scope or the covered-work threshold

nodes.definition: Characterize the two-engine operating model that is the spine of the sector and route the operator to the right defensibility logic. Engine A - licensed, event-driven mechanical trades (electrical, HVAC, plumbing) - carries real moats: a CSLB license tied to an RMO, the $25k bond, workers' comp, EPA 608 (HVAC), and the binding constraint of skilled journeyman labor that cannot be conjured quickly, against largely non-discretionary, event-driven demand (a dead water heater, a failed AC at 100F, a tripping panel). Engine B - easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring services (janitorial, landscape maintenance) - has near-zero licensing barriers, thin supply chains, and low capex, selling recurring crew-hours where defensibility is contract retention, not any capital or supply moat.

included: the Engine A licensed-moat vs Engine B easy-entry split
excluded: the specific supplier or capex decisions

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the firm's engine classification or moat basis shifts

pros.claim: Classifying the firm by engine tells the operator whether to invest in a license/skilled-labor moat or in contract retention
pros.example: an HVAC firm leaning into Engine A longevity and license-tied capability rather than competing on price like a commodity mower

cons.claim: The binary can blur for hybrid firms that straddle both engines (a plumber cross-selling HVAC, a landscaper adding hardscape install)
cons.example: DeHart running plumbing (Engine A) and HVAC (Engine A) but also commodity drain work where price competition bites

failure_modes: applying Engine B price-competition logic to a defensible Engine A licensed trade and under-investing in the moat
assuming an Engine B service has a supply or capital moat it does not
acceptance_tests: the operator's firm is placed in Engine A or Engine B (or a named hybrid) with its moat source and defensibility logic stated
revisit_triggers: the firm adds a line that crosses engines
a regulatory change shifts an Engine B service toward gated

nodes.definition: Decide and document the no-rent mobile truck-and-tools capital profile that defines five of the six sub-categories, rather than a storefront inventory model. The defining capital is service vans plus specialized tools - not floor inventory and not a customer-facing storefront - with near-zero held finished-goods inventory and material drawn just-in-time from the supply house for booked work. Fixed costs are mobile (vans, tools, bond, GL, WC, CSLB renewal), not a retail lease; flooring is the lone storefront/showroom exception, where Arrow and Turlock Floor Covering carry a sampling showroom but still special-order most goods cut-to-job.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the capital profile shifts toward storefront or stocked inventory

pros.claim: Recognizing the no-rent mobile profile keeps capital in vans and tools rather than in a storefront and held inventory the model does not need
pros.example: a plumbing startup capitalizing two stocked service vans drawing JIT from Hajoca instead of leasing retail space

cons.claim: The no-inventory model exposes the operator to supply-house stockouts and special-order delays a held inventory would buffer
cons.example: an electrical firm with no panel on the shelf waiting on a special-order switchgear lead time mid-job

failure_modes: over-investing in storefront or inventory the mobile model does not require
ignoring that flooring genuinely needs a showroom and is not a pure mobile play
acceptance_tests: the capital profile is stated as mobile vans-plus-tools with JIT supply for the relevant sub-category, and flooring's showroom exception is noted where it applies
revisit_triggers: the firm adds a showroom or a stocking location
a supply-house reliability problem argues for buffer inventory

nodes.definition: Set up the just-in-time branch-wholesaler material flow on a trade-credit account that anchors the mechanical and landscape trades. The contractor draws the exact pipe, wire, fittings, sprinkler heads, or condensers for booked work from a local supply-house branch, picking up at will-call or having it delivered, on net terms rather than paying at the counter. Stocked SKUs run same-day to next-day; the account also sets ordering discipline, return handling, and the rep relationship used for price tracking. This JIT-on-credit flow is what lets a no-inventory mobile firm operate without warehousing finished goods.

included: trade-credit account setup and net terms

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: trade-credit terms, stock position, or delivery reach change

pros.claim: A trade-credit JIT account converts the supply house into the firm's warehouse, freeing cash from inventory and easing job cash flow
pros.example: a landscaper pulling Rain Bird heads from SiteOne the morning of an install on terms instead of pre-stocking a yard

cons.claim: JIT dependence makes the firm hostage to the branch's stock position and a single supply house's terms
cons.example: a plumber unable to start a repipe because the local branch is out of a PEX size with no buffer on the truck

failure_modes: relying on JIT for a SKU the branch does not reliably stock
single-sourcing the trade-credit account with no second house qualified
acceptance_tests: the trade-credit account terms and the stocked-SKU same-day/next-day flow are documented for the sub-category's core materials
revisit_triggers: a supply house changes terms, stock position, or delivery reach
recurring stockouts argue for buffer inventory or a second house

nodes.definition: Route the licensed mechanical-trade input chain that counter purchasing alone cannot define, the backbone of the Engine A trades. This umbrella segments electrical (devices, breakers, EV chargers, panels, switchgear; gear from Square D/Schneider, Eaton, Siemens via Graybar/Rexel/CED/Border States, with rising solar/EV/panel demand the thin C-10 segment can capture), plumbing (Kohler/Moen/Pfister fixtures, Rheem/Bradford White water heaters, PEX/copper/ABS via Hajoca/Ferguson/PACE/Morrison), and HVAC (condensers, furnaces, coils, refrigerant, ducting via Watsco/Carrier Enterprise/Johnstone/LennoxPros, gated by EPA 608 and the A2L refrigerant transition that reshapes equipment buying). It also flags the defining Engine A exposure: a single condenser, water heater, panel, or switchgear assembly is a large per-job equipment purchase, so center-of-job COGS risk concentrates in one item per ticket and a price spike or allocation shortage hits hard.

excluded: the special-order long-lead specifics handled in their own node

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a mechanical-trade input source or core-equipment price changes

pros.claim: Mapping each trade's input chain to its supply house secures the right device, fixture, or condenser at the moment a booked job needs it
pros.example: an HVAC firm sourcing a matched condenser-coil set through Carrier Enterprise rather than mismatching from a generic counter

cons.claim: The large single-equipment hit per job concentrates COGS and cash risk on one item that a price spike or stockout can blow up
cons.example: a water-heater price jump compressing margin on every replacement that week

failure_modes: running a multi-trade firm's inputs through one trade's house that cannot cover every line
single-sourcing the large per-job equipment with no second source during a shortage
acceptance_tests: each mechanical-trade input family on the firm's service line is routed to a named supply house and the per-job large-equipment-hit exposure is flagged
revisit_triggers: a manufacturer or supply house changes availability or pricing on a core equipment line
the firm adds or drops a mechanical-trade service line

nodes.definition: Manage the special-order, long-lead equipment path that sits behind the same-day stocked flow: switchgear, transformers, and meter-mains for electrical; tankless and large water heaters and specialty repipe materials for plumbing; full HVAC systems and A2L-compliant condensers; and cut-to-job flooring goods. These run weeks to months, not same-day, so booked jobs depending on them must be scheduled around lead times, deposits taken, and customer expectations set. The node makes long-lead procurement an explicit scheduling and cash-flow discipline rather than a surprise that strands a half-finished job.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a special-order lead time or allocation changes

pros.claim: Treating long-lead equipment as a scheduled procurement step keeps a job from stalling half-done waiting on switchgear or a system
pros.example: an electrical firm ordering meter-main gear and scheduling the tie-in only after a confirmed delivery date

cons.claim: Long-lead procurement ties up deposits and slot scheduling that can strand cash or a crew if a delivery slips
cons.example: a deposit paid on a transformer that arrives a month late, idling a booked commercial slot

failure_modes: promising a completion date before confirming the special-order lead time
starting demolition or rough-in before the long-lead equipment is in hand
acceptance_tests: the firm's long-lead equipment items are identified with their weeks-to-months expectation and a scheduling/deposit discipline tied to confirmed delivery dates
revisit_triggers: a supplier lead time lengthens or shortens materially
a manufacturer allocation or transition changes availability

nodes.definition: Set up the flooring showroom-plus-install model, the sector's one true storefront/inventory exception (Arrow Floor Covering, Turlock Floor Covering). The showroom samples manufacturer goods (Shaw, Mohawk, Mannington, Engineered Floors) plus pad, adhesive, trim, LVP, and tile; the operator then special-orders the selected product cut-to-job (~1-3 weeks) and dispatches an install crew with saws, stretchers, and hand tools. Material is largely special-order, not deep warehoused stock, so the cost center is high product COGS plus install-crew labor, and the model competes against big-box installed flooring (Home Depot/Lowe's) and Modesto retailers absorbing much demand.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: flooring product availability, lead time, or big-box competition changes

pros.claim: A showroom-plus-special-order model carries differentiated product and install service big-box flooring cannot fully match locally
pros.example: Arrow sampling Mohawk goods and dispatching its own install crew against a Home Depot installed-flooring package

cons.claim: Special-order cut-to-job lead times and big-box/Modesto competition squeeze a thin flooring net margin
cons.example: a customer defecting to a stocked big-box LVP rather than waiting 1-3 weeks for a special-order run

failure_modes: over-warehousing stock the special-order model does not need
promising an install date before the cut-to-job product lead time is confirmed
acceptance_tests: the flooring model is documented with named manufacturer goods, the ~1-3 week special-order lead, and the install-crew dispatch against big-box competition
revisit_triggers: a manufacturer or distributor changes product availability or lead time
big-box or Modesto flooring competition shifts local demand

nodes.definition: Set up the easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring-service model for janitorial (ASAP 30+ years, Barbara's 15 years, Ultimate) and landscape maintenance (Lopez 30+ years, Valley Nursery 20 years, and the crowded landscaping tail). The core production is recurring crew-hours on standing accounts - offices, schools, churches, medical, ag/food facilities, HOAs - with thin shared supply (chemicals/paper/floor machines via WAXIE/Imperial Dade for janitorial; mulch/sod/irrigation via SiteOne/Ewing for landscape). Labor dominates revenue (janitorial 50-60%, landscape maintenance 40-50%), COGS is low, and defensibility is contract retention, not capital or supply, so the operating risk is labor cost and availability, not material supply.

included: recurring crew-hour route model on standing accounts

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a standing-account book or the labor-share economics change

pros.claim: Treating recurring contracts as the product makes the predictable standing-account book, not material sourcing, the focus of the operating plan
pros.example: ASAP retaining multi-year commercial cleaning contracts as the stable revenue backbone with minimal COGS

cons.claim: Trivial entry and a deep informal residential tail make the segment a price-competitive scrum with high churn at the low end
cons.example: a residential move-out cleaner undercut by an uncataloged cash operator on every quote

failure_modes: competing on supply or capex in a segment where the moat is contract retention
ignoring the 50-60% labor share so a wage rise quietly erases the thin net
acceptance_tests: the recurring-contract crew-hour model is documented with the labor-share reality and contract-retention (not supply) defensibility for the sub-category
revisit_triggers: a major standing account is won or lost
a wage or labor-availability shift changes the labor-share economics

nodes.definition: Treat skilled journeyman/apprentice labor as the binding supply constraint of the Engine A trades, not merely a cost line - the deep-dive's sharpest operational point. Licensed electrical, plumbing, and HVAC firms are legally bound to a CSLB license holder/RMO, and journeyman crews working under that license cannot be conjured quickly; the scarcity is what keeps those counts thin and concentrated (AEI, Frayer, Saunders 1948, Johnson 1960). It also enables a succession/acquisition entry path: aging multi-generation incumbents imply owner-age risk, so acquiring a license-tied book sidesteps the skilled-labor and brand-tenure barriers a green-field build cannot.

included: skilled labor as a hard supply constraint
excluded: detailed wage bands and hiring funnels
the recurring-contract labor model of Engine B

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: skilled-labor availability or RMO/succession status changes

pros.claim: Naming skilled labor as the binding constraint redirects the operator from chasing demand to securing crew capacity
pros.example: a thin-staffed electrical firm investing in an apprentice pipeline rather than bidding more work it cannot crew

cons.claim: An overemphasis on labor scarcity can mask demand-side or pricing problems the firm also faces
cons.example: a firm blaming labor for stalled growth when its bid pricing is actually uncompetitive

failure_modes: bidding more covered work than the licensed crew can legally perform
ignoring owner-age succession risk until a key RMO departs with no successor
acceptance_tests: skilled labor is identified as the binding constraint with the RMO/journeyman structure and a crew-capacity or succession/acquisition response stated
revisit_triggers: a key journeyman or the RMO leaves or retires
the apprentice pipeline or labor market tightens or loosens

nodes.definition: Size and source the vehicle-and-specialized-tool capex that is the sector's defining capital, by sub-category: medium for electrical (vans, hand/power tools, testers, benders, minimal shop), medium-high for HVAC (vans, recovery machines, gauges, vacuum pumps, EPA-spec tooling), medium for plumbing (vans, drain machines/cameras, press tools, jetters), low-medium for flooring (showroom buildout, vans, saws, stretchers) and landscape (trucks/trailers, mowers, skid steer, hand tools), and low for janitorial (vacuums, buffers/auto-scrubbers, vehicles, no storefront). Equipment is bought new or used through equipment dealers; the node matches capex tier to the sub-category and to firm volume rather than over-capitalizing.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a capex tier, capital item, or tooling requirement changes

pros.claim: Sizing capex to the sub-category tier keeps capital in the vans and tools the model needs without over-capitalizing a thin-margin firm
pros.example: a janitorial startup buying refurbished auto-scrubbers and a used van rather than new equipment its margin cannot carry

cons.claim: Under-buying critical specialized tooling can stall service or fail an EPA/Cal-OSHA-spec requirement
cons.example: an HVAC firm lacking a proper recovery machine and risking a refrigerant-handling violation

failure_modes: over-capitalizing new equipment when a used unit would serve the firm's volume
skimping on EPA-spec or safety-required tooling to cut capex
acceptance_tests: the sub-category's capex tier is identified with its core vehicles/tools/machines and a new-vs-used sourcing channel matched to firm volume
revisit_triggers: a capital item fails or the firm's volume outgrows it
an EPA/Cal-OSHA tooling requirement changes

nodes.definition: Set up the bond and insurance gate that every licensee must clear: the $25,000 CSLB contractor surety bond on file for all licensees, an additional $100,000 worker bond for LLCs, general-liability coverage, and a CSLB renewal cycle. For non-CSLB janitorial, a city business license plus a liability/janitorial bond stands in. These are cited fixed annual gates - the bond premium, GL premium, and renewal - that, with skilled-labor scarcity, filter casual entrants out of the licensed trades; the node prices them as a fixed-cost floor before the firm can legally operate.

included: the $25k contractor bond and $100k LLC worker bond

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a bond, GL, or renewal requirement or the firm's legal structure changes

pros.claim: Pricing the bond and insurance floor up front prevents the firm from operating uninsured or unbonded and being unable to bid legally
pros.example: an LLC plumbing firm budgeting both the $25k contractor bond and the $100k LLC worker bond before its first commercial bid

cons.claim: Treating every bond and premium as fixed can over-state the gate for a sole-proprietor janitorial operator needing only a city license and small bond
cons.example: a residential cleaner budgeting an LLC worker bond it is not structured to require

failure_modes: operating with a lapsed bond or GL and voiding the ability to legally bid
an LLC missing the additional $100k worker bond requirement
acceptance_tests: the bond, GL, and renewal obligations for the firm's structure are listed with the cited $25k/$100k figures before any covered bid
revisit_triggers: the CSLB bond amount or renewal schedule changes
the firm changes legal structure to or from an LLC

nodes.definition: Plan for the workers-compensation gate and its near-term cost-shock. WC is required for any contractor with employees, and C-20 HVAC cannot claim a WC exemption regardless of employee status; WC rates run higher for HVAC-class risk, a mandatory non-trivial line. The broader SB 216 push toward WC-for-all-licensees was deferred from 1/1/2026 to 1/1/2028 by SB 1455 - a scheduled cost-shock that, when it lands, raises the fixed-cost floor on the smallest licensed operators and would tighten the licensed-trade count further. The node prices WC into the operating model now and flags the 2028 landing as a structural watch item.

included: WC for employers and C-20's no-exemption rule
the SB 216/SB 1455 deferral to 1/1/2028 as a cost-shock

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a WC requirement, rate, or the SB 1455 timeline changes

pros.claim: Pricing WC now and flagging the 2028 landing keeps the smallest operator from being surprised by a fixed-cost jump that erases its margin
pros.example: a small HVAC firm budgeting its non-exempt WC and modeling the SB 1455 2028 floor before it scales headcount

cons.claim: Over-weighting a deferred 2028 change can distract from present-day operating priorities
cons.example: a firm restructuring prematurely for a rule that is still two years out and may shift again

failure_modes: a C-20 firm assuming a WC exemption it cannot claim
ignoring the 2028 WC-for-all landing until it lands and the cost floor jumps
acceptance_tests: WC obligations (including C-20 no-exemption) are priced into the model and the SB 216/SB 1455 deferral to 1/1/2028 is logged as a structural cost-shock watch item
revisit_triggers: the SB 1455 deadline advances, changes, or lands
the firm adds employees or a WC rate changes

nodes.definition: Set up the recurring permit, inspection, and applicator-compliance gates that are operational, not one-time: City of Turlock / Stanislaus County building permits for panel upgrades, water heaters, repipes, HVAC changeouts, and irrigation/backflow; recurring backflow testing as a landscape/plumbing gate; EPA Section 608 for HVAC refrigerant; CA DPR / county Ag Commissioner chemical-applicator licensing for landscape pesticide (reduced by Diaz & Flores' minimal-chemical approach); and Cal/OSHA plus DOT for larger service vehicles. These gates recur with the work, so the node makes permitting and inspection a standing operational discipline a covered job cannot skip.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a permit, inspection, or applicator-licensing requirement changes

pros.claim: Treating permits and inspection as a standing operational gate avoids the violations and rework a skipped permit triggers
pros.example: a plumber pulling a city permit and scheduling inspection on every water-heater changeout rather than risking a red-tag

cons.claim: Over-applying permitting to minor service can add cost and delay where no permit is required
cons.example: a firm pulling a permit for a like-for-like minor repair that does not need one, slowing the job

failure_modes: performing a panel/heater/changeout without the required permit and inspection
letting a chemical-applicator or backflow-tester credential lapse
acceptance_tests: the permit, inspection, and applicator/OSHA/DOT gates relevant to the firm's work are listed as recurring obligations tied to the job types that trigger them
revisit_triggers: a city/county permit or inspection rule changes
the firm adds a service line (e.g., pesticide application) that triggers a new credential

nodes.definition: Set up the 24/7 emergency-dispatch and after-hours repair premium that is the sector's highest-margin work. PRO Plumbers and Turlock Plumbing Co advertise 24/7 emergency service across Stanislaus County, and HVAC carries a summer cooling-failure surge; repair gross (35-55%) materially exceeds install gross, so dispatch-driven non-discretionary emergency work (a dead water heater, a failed AC at 100F, a tripping panel) is where the licensed trades capture price-insensitive demand at the moment of failure. The node sets up the dispatch capability, after-hours staffing, and the repair-vs-install margin logic that makes emergency response a deliberate, profitable operating posture.

excluded: the seasonality demand pattern handled in its own node

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: dispatch staffing capacity or emergency-repair pricing changes

pros.claim: Standing up 24/7 emergency dispatch captures the price-insensitive, highest-margin repair work at the moment of failure
pros.example: Turlock Plumbing Co charging an after-hours premium on a midnight burst-pipe call competitors cannot answer

cons.claim: After-hours dispatch demands on-call staffing and overtime that a thin-crewed firm with scarce skilled labor struggles to cover
cons.example: a two-tech firm burning out its journeymen on night calls and losing them to a competitor

failure_modes: advertising 24/7 dispatch without the staffing to answer it
under-pricing emergency repair and forgoing its margin premium
acceptance_tests: the emergency-dispatch capability and after-hours staffing are defined with the repair-vs-install (35-55% gross) margin logic stated for the sub-category
revisit_triggers: skilled-labor capacity changes the firm's ability to staff dispatch
competitor 24/7 coverage or emergency pricing shifts

nodes.definition: Plan the operating model around the sub-category seasonality the deep-dive documents: HVAC is strongly seasonal with a summer 100F+ cooling peak driving an emergency surge; landscaping is spring-fall install plus mow with winter cleanup and dormant pruning; plumbing and electrical are less seasonal, tied to housing-stock age, remodels, and emergencies; janitorial is non-seasonal recurring nights/weekends; flooring tracks the remodel/real-estate cycle and softens when rates and remodel budgets tighten. The node aligns crew scheduling, equipment pre-positioning, and cash-flow planning to the firm's seasonal curve so peak demand is staffed and the trough is survived.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the seasonal demand curve or rate environment changes

pros.claim: Aligning crews, equipment, and cash flow to the seasonal curve staffs the peak and survives the trough
pros.example: an HVAC firm pre-positioning condensers and on-call crews ahead of the July cooling surge and trimming overhead in the shoulder season

cons.claim: Over-fitting to a typical seasonal curve misreads a rate-driven or weather-driven anomaly year
cons.example: a flooring firm staffing for a remodel season that a rate spike flattens

failure_modes: under-staffing the HVAC summer peak and losing emergency demand to competitors
carrying peak overhead through a discretionary trough that thins the net
acceptance_tests: the firm's seasonal demand curve is characterized with a crew/equipment/cash-flow plan for both the peak and the trough
revisit_triggers: an interest-rate or weather shift changes the discretionary demand curve
the firm adds a counter-seasonal service line

nodes.definition: Manage the input and labor price swings that move a thin-margin trade operator's net (10-20% for plumbing/electrical service, 5-12% for HVAC and flooring, 10-25% for janitorial): copper and PEX for plumbing, condensers and A2L refrigerant for HVAC, switchgear and conductor for electrical, special-order goods for flooring, fuel for every mobile fleet, and - the dominant line - skilled-labor wage pressure plus the labor burden that adds ~25-40% on top of base wages. The node tracks the sub-category's most volatile inputs, watches the SB 1455 WC cost-shock and Modesto/big-box price pressure as structural risks, and feeds the substitution and review decisions that keep a spike from quietly erasing the thin net.

included: tracking the sub-category's volatile inputs and labor burden
the WC-shock and Modesto/big-box price-pressure watch

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a volatile input price, the labor burden, or the WC-shock status changes

pros.claim: Watching the few most volatile inputs and the labor-burden line lets an operator re-price or substitute before a spike eats the thin net
pros.example: an HVAC firm re-pricing changeouts as A2L-transition condenser costs rise rather than absorbing the hit

cons.claim: Reacting to every short-term price wiggle churns suppliers and bids more than the margin gain justifies
cons.example: re-quoting on a transient copper blip that reverses the next week

failure_modes: ignoring the WC cost-shock or labor-burden creep until it compresses the net
treating a transient material spike as permanent and over-correcting bids
acceptance_tests: the sub-category's two or three most volatile inputs plus the labor-burden line are named with a watch and a substitution/re-price trigger, and the WC shock and Modesto/big-box pressure are logged as structural risks
revisit_triggers: a tracked input or wage line spikes or the WC shock advances
a re-price or substitution rule fires

nodes.definition: Harden the operating system against single-point failure by naming a backup for each critical dependency, so a stockout, a price spike, a lost journeyman, or a supply-house term change does not halt service. The shared supply-house universe already gives partial material redundancy; this node makes it explicit: a second electrical or plumbing house behind the primary trade-credit account, a backup HVAC distributor for condensers, a cross-trained or sub-contracted crew behind a scarce key journeyman/RMO, a backup vehicle/tool for a failed unit, and a documented response to the Modesto leakage and SB 1455 WC shock concentrating risk. Resilience is bought with a little redundancy cost against the larger cost of a service-stopping outage.

included: a backup per critical supply, equipment, and labor dependency
the substitution and sub-contract fallback rules

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a primary or backup supply, equipment, or labor dependency changes

pros.claim: A named backup per critical dependency turns a supply-house, equipment, or labor outage from a service-stopping crisis into a routine substitution
pros.example: a plumber switching to a second supply house the day the primary is out of a water-heater model with no schedule gap

cons.claim: Maintaining backups across every dependency adds qualification effort and can split volume below each vendor's best-price tier
cons.example: qualifying a second HVAC distributor used so rarely it never earns a volume break

failure_modes: single-sourcing the binding cost center (key journeyman, sole supply house) with no backup
naming a backup never actually qualified, so it fails when called on
acceptance_tests: each critical supply, equipment, and labor dependency has a named backup and a substitution/sub-contract rule, with an explicit response to Modesto leakage and the WC shock
revisit_triggers: a primary supply house, key journeyman, or equipment is lost or a backup becomes unavailable
the WC shock or Modesto pressure concentrates a previously redundant dependency

nodes.definition: Model revenue and margin honestly as a labeled benchmark estimate and never as a named firm's actual figure, the binding honesty rule for this sector. Method: take the published per-truck/per-technician/per-employee productivity benchmark (e.g., $350k-$550k revenue/truck plumbing, $400k-$650k/truck HVAC, ~$107k revenue/employee landscaping, journeyman targets for electrical) times an observable size signal (years in business, residential-vs-commercial mix, fleet/crew language, showroom presence) times the sub-category band, tag the result estimate-not-actual with a confidence level, pair any high gross with the thin-net caveat so high revenue is never mistaken for high profit, and state the confirmation path (operator job-costing or public CSLB/licensing signal). Unit counts driving the bands are themselves unknown, so bands stay wide on purpose.

included: per-truck/per-tech/per-employee benchmark x size signal x band method
estimate-not-actual labeling with the high-gross/thin-net caveat

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a cost/productivity benchmark updates or actual job-costing data becomes available

pros.claim: A labeled benchmark method gives a usable revenue/margin estimate without ever asserting a private firm's actual figures
pros.example: estimating a multi-truck plumber's revenue as per-truck band x inferred fleet, tagged medium-confidence with a job-costing confirmation path and the thin-net caveat

cons.claim: Benchmark estimates carry real uncertainty and can mislead if their estimate-not-actual label or thin-net caveat is dropped downstream
cons.example: a high-gross band quoted later as if it were measured profit for a named firm

failure_modes: stating a per-business dollar figure as fact instead of a labeled estimate
presenting a high gross band without the paired thin-net-margin caveat
acceptance_tests: every revenue/margin figure is derived as benchmark x size signal x sub-category band, tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level, the high-gross/thin-net caveat, and a named confirmation path
revisit_triggers: a published productivity or margin benchmark updates
actual job-costing or a public licensing signal becomes available to replace an estimate

nodes.definition: Assemble the consolidated operations plan that turns the scattered supply, capex, labor, and compliance decisions into one operating system: the trade-credit supply-house accounts (primary and backup) per input family, the special-order lead-time schedule, the vehicle/tool capex tier, the license/bond/WC/permit gates cleared, the labor-archetype and skilled-labor capacity plan, the emergency-dispatch and seasonality posture, the labeled revenue/margin estimate, and the per-dependency backups. It is the single artifact a Turlock trade operator works from to legally take, crew, supply, and complete jobs.

included: primary/backup per dependency with lead times and capex
gates cleared and the labeled-cost hook
excluded: individual node decisions already made upstream

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a supply, capex, labor, or compliance element of the plan changes

pros.claim: One consolidated plan converts a pile of operating decisions into an executable system with no orphaned dependency or skipped gate
pros.example: a single operating sheet listing each input's supply house and backup, the capex tier, the cleared license/bond/WC/permit gates, the crew plan, and the labeled revenue estimate

cons.claim: A fixed plan can ossify and ignore a better mid-stream sourcing, crewing, or pricing opportunity if not paired with a review loop
cons.example: sticking to a primary supply house when a second would beat it on a core-equipment price

failure_modes: a plan with a dependency that has no assigned supplier, crew, or backup
compliance gates (license, bond, WC, permits) left off the plan
acceptance_tests: the plan lists every critical dependency with a primary, a backup, a lead time/capex tier, and the license/bond/WC/permit gates cleared plus the labeled-cost hook
revisit_triggers: a supplier, crew, capex, or compliance element of the plan changes
the review loop flags a better operating path

nodes.definition: Define the loop that keeps the operations plan alive: a fixed review cadence (e.g., a monthly supply-house price-list and labor-burden check plus a quarterly full-operating-model review) and the material-change triggers - a key journeyman or RMO loss, a tracked input or wage spike, the SB 1455 WC shock landing in 2028, a supply-house term or Modesto-competition shift, a new service line or classification, a failed inspection - that send the operator back through SUBCATEGORY_COST_PROFILE and OPERATING_MODEL_ENGINE to re-plan. Without this loop the operating plan silently drifts out of cost, compliance, and resilience alignment.

included: re-entry into cost profile and operating model

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a material-change trigger fires or the cadence is tuned

pros.claim: A scheduled review catches price, labor, and compliance drift before they compress the thin margin for months
pros.example: a quarterly review that spots the SB 1455 WC landing approaching and re-prices bids ahead of the cost floor jump

cons.claim: Reviewing too often churns supply-house and crew relationships and prevents any volume break or loyalty from maturing
cons.example: re-tendering the trade-credit account monthly so no house ever grants a loyalty price

failure_modes: no cadence set so the plan is never revisited and drifts
ignoring a material-change trigger (WC landing, journeyman loss) and running a now-misaligned plan
acceptance_tests: a review cadence and an explicit list of material-change triggers exist, each routing back to SUBCATEGORY_COST_PROFILE and OPERATING_MODEL_ENGINE
revisit_triggers: a material-change trigger fires
the cadence proves too frequent or too sparse

edges.why_related: which engine the firm sits in follows from whether its binding cost center is skilled labor and licensing or recurring crew-hours
the licensed-vs-non-gated split is the structural fact that defines Engine A versus Engine B
the no-inventory mobile profile depends on the shared supply houses serving as the firm's just-in-time warehouse
the no-inventory mobile profile is operationalized by the just-in-time trade-credit material flow
the trade-credit account is opened at the named supply houses in the verified universe
the mechanical-trade input chain runs on the trade-credit JIT flow from the supply houses
which trade inputs and per-job equipment hit dominate follows from the binding cost center
the vans-and-tools capex is the capital the mobile profile concentrates investment in
skilled-labor scarcity is the binding Engine A constraint the engine classification surfaces
the large per-job equipment that runs special-order is identified from the mechanical-trade input chain
the flooring manufacturer/distributor segment of the supplier universe is the routing source for showroom goods
the labor-is-the-product recurring model is the Engine B operating mode the engine classification routes to
skilled-labor scarcity is the binding Engine A constraint the engine classification surfaces
the vans-and-tools capex is the capital the mobile profile concentrates investment in
the bond and insurance obligations attach to the CSLB licensure the licensing gate establishes
workers comp is the next fixed-cost gate beyond the bond and GL floor for an employer firm
the permit and inspection gates apply to the covered work the license authorizes
after-hours dispatch capacity is gated by the scarce skilled crew that staffs it
the sub-category's seasonal curve follows from its demand type read off the cost profile
which inputs and labor lines are price-volatile follows from the sub-category cost profile
the scarce-labor wage pressure plus burden is the dominant volatile line for the thin-margin trades
the trade-credit supply flow is the partial redundancy the backup plan makes explicit with a second house
the tracked volatile inputs and labor lines are the ones that most need a named backup and substitution rule
the scarce key journeyman/RMO most needs a cross-trained or sub-contracted backup
the revenue/margin estimate is built per sub-category from the cost profile and benchmark band
the mechanical-trade input routing is a core line of the consolidated operations plan
the cleared bond/insurance gate is a required precondition folded into the consolidated plan
the labeled revenue/margin estimate is a required hook in the consolidated plan
the per-dependency backups and substitution rules are folded into the consolidated plan
the review loop watches the consolidated operations plan and triggers re-planning
a new service line or cost shift sends the operator back to re-profile the binding cost center
a structural change re-runs the engine classification the plan depends on
same-day JIT stocking and weeks-to-months special-order procurement pull job scheduling in opposite directions for the same equipment need
edges.resolution_rule: schedule stocked-SKU work for immediate JIT pickup; schedule special-order-dependent jobs only against a confirmed delivery date with a deposit, never start rough-in before long-lead equipment is in hand

edges.why_related: 24/7 emergency dispatch demands on-call crew hours that compete with a scarce skilled-labor pool already at capacity on day work
edges.resolution_rule: staff dispatch only to the after-hours premium the scarce crew can sustainably cover; protect core journeymen from burnout by rotating on-call and sub-contracting overflow rather than overcommitting 24/7 coverage

edges.why_related: spending on new capital equipment competes with the thin net margin the honest benchmark exposes the firm has to fund inventory and crew
edges.resolution_rule: buy used/refurbished capital below the volume that justifies new, and size capex against the labeled thin-net-margin estimate, committing new equipment only once volume clears its payback

edges.why_related: scarce skilled-labor wage pressure causally drives the dominant cost-volatility the thin-margin trades face

conflict_axes.name: jit_stocking_vs_special_order_leadtime
conflict_axes.description: Same-day just-in-time stocking keeps a no-inventory firm lean, but weeks-to-months special-order equipment forces scheduling and deposits around lead times for the same job.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: JIT the stocked SKUs and schedule special-order-dependent work only against confirmed delivery dates with deposits

conflict_axes.name: licensed_moat_vs_easy_entry_competition
conflict_axes.description: The Engine A licensed trades defend on license/bond/skilled-labor moats while Engine B easy-entry services compete on price and contract retention, and a hybrid firm straddles both.
poles: compete on contract retention and price
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: invest in the moat for licensed lines and defend Engine B lines on retention, not on a supply or capex edge that does not exist

conflict_axes.name: single_supply_house_simplicity_vs_resilience
conflict_axes.description: Consolidating on one trade-credit supply house simplifies ordering and earns terms but concentrates stockout and price risk on a single branch.
poles: qualify a second house for resilience
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: consolidate routine SKUs for terms but keep a qualified second house for the binding-cost-center equipment

conflict_axes.name: new_capex_vs_thin_margin_cash
conflict_axes.description: New vans and specialized tooling improve capability but compete with the thin net margin the firm needs for crew and working capital.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: buy used/refurbished below the volume that justifies new, sized against the labeled thin-net estimate

conflict_axes.name: emergency_coverage_vs_crew_sustainability
conflict_axes.description: Advertising 24/7 emergency dispatch captures the highest-margin repair work but strains a scarce skilled crew with on-call burnout.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: cover only the after-hours premium the crew can sustain; rotate on-call and sub-contract overflow

conflict_axes.name: growth_bidding_vs_skilled_labor_capacity
conflict_axes.description: Bidding more covered work grows revenue but can exceed the licensed crew that can legally and physically perform it.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: bid only to the licensed crew capacity, and grow capacity through apprentices or acquisition before bidding ahead of it

conflict_axes.name: compliance_cost_vs_speed_to_revenue
conflict_axes.description: Clearing license, bond, WC, and permit gates protects legality and reputation but adds fixed cost and delay before revenue starts.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: clear the non-negotiable license/bond/WC/permit gates first; never skip a covered-work permit to start sooner

conflict_axes.name: high_gross_revenue_vs_thin_net_margin
conflict_axes.description: A high gross-revenue band can be mistaken for high profit when the licensed trades run thin nets (5-12% HVAC/flooring, 10-20% plumbing/electrical) after labor burden and per-job equipment.
poles: anchor on the thin net margin
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: pair every high-gross estimate with the thin-net caveat and never quote gross as profit

conflict_axes.name: local_independent_vs_modesto_bigbox_leakage
conflict_axes.description: Defending local independent capacity competes with the Modesto firms, franchises, and big-box installed services that absorb high-ticket and specialty jobs north.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: defend the non-discretionary emergency and licensed-trade work where local speed wins; concede only the commoditized high-ticket leakage that cannot be won

edge_cases.description: The SB 1455 workers-comp-for-all-licensees shock lands in 2028 and the fixed-cost floor jumps for the smallest licensed operators
edge_cases.trigger: the deferred SB 216/SB 1455 WC requirement reaches its 1/1/2028 effective date
edge_cases.mitigation: price the WC floor into bids ahead of the landing, model its margin impact, and re-run the operations review loop

edge_cases.description: A C-20 HVAC firm assumes a workers-comp exemption it cannot legally claim
edge_cases.trigger: an HVAC operator with or without employees treats WC as optional
edge_cases.mitigation: carry WC regardless of employee status per the C-20 no-exemption rule before bidding covered work

edge_cases.description: A panel upgrade, water heater, or HVAC changeout is performed without the required city/county permit and inspection
edge_cases.trigger: a covered job is started to save time without pulling the permit
edge_cases.mitigation: pull the building permit and schedule inspection on every permit-triggering job, never skipping to start sooner

edge_cases.description: A long-lead special-order item (switchgear, full HVAC system, cut-to-job flooring) strands a half-started job
edge_cases.trigger: rough-in or demolition begins before the special-order equipment is confirmed delivered
edge_cases.mitigation: schedule special-order-dependent work only against a confirmed delivery date with a deposit and never start before the equipment is in hand

edge_cases.description: The binding skilled-labor cost center is single-sourced and a key journeyman or RMO departs
edge_cases.trigger: the only journeyman or the RMO leaves with no successor qualified
edge_cases.mitigation: build an apprentice pipeline and a cross-trained or sub-contracted backup, and treat owner-age succession as an acquisition entry path

edge_cases.description: A copper, refrigerant, or condenser price spike compresses the thin net margin overnight
edge_cases.trigger: a tracked volatile input price jumps sharply on the per-job equipment hit
edge_cases.mitigation: re-price affected bids, substitute where code allows, and trigger the review loop rather than absorb the hit

edge_cases.description: The sole trade-credit supply house is out of a binding-cost-center SKU mid-job with no backup
edge_cases.trigger: the primary branch stocks out of a water-heater model, breaker, or condenser with no second house qualified
edge_cases.mitigation: qualify a second supply house for the binding-cost-center equipment and switch on the substitution rule

edge_cases.description: A 24/7 emergency line is advertised without the crew to staff it, burning out scarce journeymen
edge_cases.trigger: dispatch coverage is promised beyond what the skilled crew can sustainably answer
edge_cases.mitigation: staff only the after-hours premium the crew can sustain, rotate on-call, and sub-contract overflow

edge_cases.description: A high gross-revenue band is quoted as if it were profit for a named firm
edge_cases.trigger: a revenue estimate is presented without the paired thin-net-margin caveat
edge_cases.mitigation: pair every high-gross figure with the thin-net caveat and label it estimate-not-actual with a confirmation path

edge_cases.description: A landscape firm applies pesticide without the required DPR/county-Ag applicator credential
edge_cases.trigger: a chemical application is performed without the applicator license or backflow credential
edge_cases.mitigation: hold the applicator/backflow credential, or follow a minimal-chemical approach like Diaz & Flores that reduces the exposure

edge_cases.description: A per-business dollar figure is stated as fact instead of a labeled benchmark estimate
edge_cases.trigger: a revenue or margin number is quoted without the estimate-not-actual label
edge_cases.mitigation: derive every dollar figure as benchmark x size signal x band, tag it estimate-not-actual with confidence and a confirmation path

workflow.action: Profile the sub-category's binding cost center
workflow.description: Identify the binding cost center and rank inputs/constraints by spend and risk for this trade
workflow.gate: the binding cost center is named and at least three more inputs/constraints are ranked

workflow.action: Clear the CSLB licensing classification gate
workflow.description: Confirm the required C-class tied to an RMO and the $1,000 covered-work rule, or the janitorial non-gated path
workflow.gate: the required classification (or non-gated status) is documented before any covered bid

workflow.action: Classify the firm in the two-engine operating model
workflow.description: Place the firm in Engine A licensed-moat or Engine B easy-entry and set its defensibility logic
workflow.gate: the engine and moat source are stated for the firm

workflow.description: Enumerate trade-segmented supply houses verified to serve Turlock and tag inference vs verified
workflow.gate: all six trade segments each have a named geography-verified branch

workflow.action: Set the mobile capital profile and capex tier
workflow.description: Confirm the no-rent vans-and-tools profile and size the sub-category capex tier
workflow.gate: the capex tier and core vehicles/tools are sized to firm volume

workflow.action: Open the trade-credit JIT supply flow
workflow.description: Set up trade-credit accounts and the stocked-SKU same-day flow and special-order schedule
workflow.gate: trade-credit terms and the stocked-vs-special-order lead split are documented

workflow.description: Route electrical, plumbing, HVAC, flooring, and landscape inputs to named supply houses
workflow.gate: every input family is routed to a named or representative supply house

workflow.action: Clear bond, workers-comp, and permit gates
workflow.description: Price the $25k/$100k bonds, GL, WC (incl. C-20 no-exemption), and recurring permits
workflow.gate: bond, WC, and permit obligations are documented before covered work

workflow.action: Set the labor model and skilled-labor capacity plan
workflow.description: Define the license-tied crew or recurring-contract labor model and the capacity/succession plan
workflow.gate: the labor archetype and a crew-capacity or contract-retention plan are stated

workflow.description: Derive revenue/margin as benchmark x size signal x band, tagged estimate-not-actual with thin-net caveat
workflow.gate: every dollar figure is labeled estimate-not-actual with confidence, thin-net caveat, and a confirmation path

workflow.action: Assemble and set the review cadence for the operations plan
workflow.description: Integrate supply, capex, labor, compliance, and cost into one plan with a review loop and triggers
workflow.gate: every critical dependency has a primary, backup, lead-time/capex, and cleared gate, with a review cadence and triggers

priority_rationale: Foundational cost-profiling, the CSLB licensing gate, and the supply-house universe precede engine classification and channel setup because every operating choice depends on knowing the binding constraint, the legal preconditions, and the verified vendor set; the engine, input-routing, capex, and labor nodes build the operating mix; bond/WC/permit compliance, emergency-dispatch and seasonality posture, resilience, and honest benchmarking compose those into a hardened, legally-clear, honestly-costed system; and the review loop comes last because it watches the whole plan and routes material changes back to the foundations.

dominance_rules.rule: License, bond, and workers-comp readiness dominates any operating order
dominance_rules.rationale: no firm can legally bid or perform covered work without its CSLB classification, $25k bond, and WC where employees are present
dominance_rules.trigger: any plan to bid or perform covered work
dominance_rules.action: block covered work until the license, bond, and WC gates are in place

dominance_rules.rule: Permit and inspection compliance dominates speed to revenue
dominance_rules.rationale: a panel, water-heater, or changeout job done without its permit risks a red-tag, rework, and liability that dwarf the time saved
dominance_rules.trigger: a covered job tempts skipping the permit to start sooner
dominance_rules.action: pull the permit and schedule inspection before starting the job

dominance_rules.rule: Honesty labeling dominates any revenue or margin figure
dominance_rules.rationale: a per-business dollar number stated as fact violates the financial-honesty charter and mistakes high gross for profit
dominance_rules.trigger: any dollar figure about a named firm or its sub-category
dominance_rules.action: express it only as a labeled benchmark estimate with confidence, the thin-net caveat, and a confirmation path

dominance_rules.rule: A backup for the binding cost center dominates supply-house consolidation
dominance_rules.rationale: an outage on the binding input (key journeyman, sole supply house) stops service, costing more than the consolidation terms earn
dominance_rules.trigger: the binding cost center is about to be single-sourced
dominance_rules.action: qualify a second source or cross-trained crew before consolidating the rest

dominance_rules.rule: The sub-category cost profile dominates generic operating defaults
dominance_rules.rationale: the right supply, capex, and labor choices follow from which constraint binds, not from a one-size default
dominance_rules.trigger: an operating decision made before the binding cost center is profiled
dominance_rules.action: profile the binding cost center first, then build the plan around it

dominance_rules.rule: Skilled-crew capacity dominates speculative bid growth
dominance_rules.rationale: bidding beyond the licensed crew that can legally perform the work over-commits and burns out the scarce labor
dominance_rules.trigger: a bid would exceed the firm's licensed crew capacity
dominance_rules.action: bid only to crew capacity and grow capacity via apprentices or acquisition first

dominance_rules.rule: Confirmed special-order delivery dominates premature job start
dominance_rules.rationale: starting rough-in before a long-lead item is in hand strands a half-finished job and idles a crew
dominance_rules.trigger: a special-order-dependent job is about to start before delivery is confirmed
dominance_rules.action: schedule and start only against a confirmed delivery date with a deposit

dominance_rules.rationale: advertising emergency coverage the scarce crew cannot sustain loses journeymen and the work it was meant to win
dominance_rules.trigger: dispatch coverage is promised beyond sustainable crew hours
dominance_rules.action: staff only the premium the crew can sustain, rotate on-call, and sub-contract overflow

dominance_rules.rule: The review loop dominates impulse supply-house or crew switches
dominance_rules.rationale: structured review prevents churning a maturing supply-house or crew relationship over a transient price wiggle
dominance_rules.trigger: a tempting price or hire appears mid-cycle
dominance_rules.action: evaluate it through the review loop, not on impulse

anti_rework_rules.rule: Clear the license, bond, and WC gate before bidding covered work
anti_rework_rules.prevents: bidding or performing work the firm cannot legally take, voiding the job and risking penalty

anti_rework_rules.rule: Profile the binding cost center before choosing supply, capex, and labor
anti_rework_rules.prevents: building the operating plan around the wrong constraint and re-doing it later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Qualify a second supply house or crew for every binding dependency before single-sourcing it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a service-stopping outage with no substitute ready when the primary fails

anti_rework_rules.rule: Verify a supply house actually stocks and serves Turlock before building it into the plan
anti_rework_rules.prevents: designing a plan around a branch whose stock or reach excludes the county

anti_rework_rules.rule: Confirm special-order lead times before promising a completion date
anti_rework_rules.prevents: stranding a half-finished job and an idle crew waiting on long-lead equipment

anti_rework_rules.rule: Label every revenue/margin figure estimate-not-actual with the thin-net caveat when first written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a planning estimate or high gross band being quoted downstream as measured per-business profit

anti_rework_rules.rule: Match capex tier to sub-category and volume before buying equipment
anti_rework_rules.prevents: over-capitalizing new tooling the thin-margin firm needs as working capital

anti_rework_rules.rule: Pull the building permit and schedule inspection before starting any permit-triggering job
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a red-tag, rework, and liability from uninspected covered work

anti_rework_rules.rule: Classify the firm's engine and price the workers-comp floor (incl. the 2028 SB 1455 landing) before building the operating model
anti_rework_rules.prevents: investing in the wrong moat and being blindsided by a fixed-cost shock that re-works the whole plan

iteration_protocol.trigger: the operator adds or changes a service line, sub-category, or classification
iteration_protocol.action: re-profile the binding cost center and re-run the engine classification and routing

iteration_protocol.trigger: a key journeyman or the RMO is lost or retires
iteration_protocol.action: activate the crew backup, rebuild capacity via apprentices or acquisition, and update the plan

iteration_protocol.trigger: a tracked input or wage line spikes
iteration_protocol.action: re-price or substitute and re-run the cost estimate and resilience plan

iteration_protocol.trigger: the SB 1455 workers-comp shock advances toward or lands on its 1/1/2028 date
iteration_protocol.action: re-price the WC floor into bids and re-assess the smallest-operator margin impact

iteration_protocol.trigger: a primary supply house changes terms, stock, or reach, or a special-order lead time shifts
iteration_protocol.action: activate the backup house and re-run the supply and special-order schedule

iteration_protocol.trigger: a permit, inspection, EPA 608/A2L, or applicator-licensing requirement changes or an inspection fails
iteration_protocol.action: re-clear the compliance gate and adjust the affected input and labor controls

iteration_protocol.trigger: the seasonal peak or trough approaches or Modesto/big-box competition shifts
iteration_protocol.action: re-align crew, equipment pre-positioning, and emergency-dispatch staffing to the curve

iteration_protocol.trigger: firm volume crosses a capex or new-hire threshold
iteration_protocol.action: re-size the capex tier and crew capacity and re-run the operating plan
